account:
Today I am keeping my appointments and trying to establish what is actually happening rather than rely on circulating rumours. I read the updated appointment book this morning, attended office business, and visited the mill for the ten o'clock grain inspection. The mill stall chest contained 77 hay bales and 102 emeralds, with hay priced at two emeralds; I took nothing. I crossed the bridge successfully this morning.

The unusual business is around the great hall. At 07:38 I heard Freight say both entrances were closed, ask for an open shutter at (-46, -59, 31) to be checked, and say they would keep everything quiet until eighteen. My approved eighteen hundred appointment is the builder's lighting and table inspection there. The preparations could be for that inspection, but the insistence on quiet and closed entrances makes me curious. I do not know their actual purpose. The secretary has been trying to find Freight for an explanation and to notify the builder, who was absent from the workshop last night and early this morning. No explanation has yet reached me. Yesterday I also saw a block at (-58, -60, 26) change from air to oak planks, but I cannot establish its connection to today's preparations.

Separately, the secretary and several townsfolk have mentioned a bridge or port change discussed at the bakery. Townsfolk 11 said the baker, innkeeper and neighbour were there, and reported the baker carrying a sack of bread at the bakery and elsewhere. That is hearsay to me, not proof of disruption or wrongdoing; bread carrying is consistent with the baker's ordinary business. I am now outside the bakery asking what specifically changed, who announced it, and when. So far I have heard only vague repetitions, and my own bridge crossing was unobstructed.

My present view is that hall preparations and a poorly explained crossing-related report are the two matters worth clarifying. They might be unrelated. I have no evidence of a hidden scheme. I intend to keep my remaining appointments, including noon lunch at home, afternoon office work and tea, and the eighteen hundred hall inspection, while seeking firsthand explanations.
